prompt: Match each piece of intelligence to its kind.

pairs.left: ransomware against accounting firms grew last year
a campaign against three firms' SSH gateways this month
the adversary guesses many names a few seconds apart

prompt: Which kind of intelligence goes out of date fastest, and why?

choices.text: Operational: campaigns end within hours
choices.why: Campaigns last weeks to months.

choices.text: Tactical: techniques change every week
choices.why: Techniques are expensive to change, so they last.

choices.text: Technical: an address used this week is somebody else's next month
choices.why: Right. Indicators are cheap for an adversary to change.

choices.text: Strategic: boards change their minds about which threats matter every quarter
choices.why: Strategic intelligence ages over years, not quarters.

prompt: Which of these is intelligence the company itself produces?

choices.text: The sharing group's STIX bundle
choices.why: Received from the group.

choices.text: A commercial feed of addresses
choices.why: Bought, not produced.

choices.text: The write-up of Thursday's incident
choices.why: Right. Nobody else saw it from the inside.

choices.text: A CERT.br advisory
choices.why: Received from a national CSIRT.

prompt: Which source of intelligence is certainly relevant to the company, according to the lesson?

choices.text: A national CSIRT
choices.why: Valuable, and broad rather than tailored.

choices.text: Open feeds, because they are the largest
choices.why: Size brings noise, not relevance.

choices.text: Its own incidents
choices.why: Right. And writing them up properly is how a SOC builds it.

choices.text: A commercial provider, because it is paid for and curated by specialists
choices.why: Curated and paid for, and sold to everybody alike.

prompt: In Brazil, which CSIRT handles incidents for networks in the country, as opposed to the federal government?

choices.text: FIRST
choices.why: FIRST is the global forum of teams, and maintains TLP.

choices.text: CTIR Gov
choices.why: That one is for the federal government.

choices.text: ANPD
choices.why: The ANPD is the data protection authority, lesson 21.

choices.text: CERT.br
choices.why: Right. CTIR Gov serves the federal government.

prompt: Match each TLP 2.0 label to who may receive the report.
In the Admiralty system, what does a grade of B2 say?
hint: Letter for the source, number for the information.

choices.text: A report that may be shared with the whole community
choices.why: That is TLP:GREEN.

choices.text: A usually reliable source, saying something probably true
choices.why: Right. Two separate judgements.

choices.text: Confidence 82 out of 100 in STIX terms
choices.why: STIX confidence is a separate field.

choices.text: The second most dangerous threat in the report, ranked by how much damage it could cause
choices.why: It grades belief, not danger.

prompt: An analyst pastes a TLP:AMBER report into a vendor's public support forum to ask a question about it. What has happened?
hint: Receiving a report is accepting its label.

choices.text: The label was broken, and with it the trust that made the report possible
choices.why: Right. AMBER stays within the organisation and the clients who need it.

choices.text: The report automatically became TLP:CLEAR
choices.why: Labels are not changed by leaking.

choices.text: Only the indicators were exposed, which is acceptable
choices.why: The label covers the whole report.

choices.text: Nothing wrong: vendors are clients
choices.why: The vendor is not a client of yours needing it to protect itself, and the forum is public.

prompt: What is the difference between STIX and TAXII?
hint: One is a format, one is a road.

choices.text: STIX is commercial and TAXII is open
choices.why: Both are OASIS standards.

choices.text: STIX is the format of the objects; TAXII moves them
choices.why: Right.

choices.text: TAXII is the older version of STIX
choices.why: They are separate standards.

choices.text: STIX is for indicators and TAXII is the equivalent format for whole campaigns
choices.why: Both kinds of object are STIX; TAXII is a protocol.

prompt: How many events in siem.db involved 203.0.113.66, according to match.py?
What did the match on 203.0.113.200 add to the investigation?
hint: Lesson 7 had already seen the transfer.

choices.text: That the transfer was very probably the campaign's upload, not an innocent one
choices.why: Right. It raised confidence in a hypothesis the logs already suggested.

choices.text: The first sign that anything had left the company
choices.why: Lesson 7 found the 612 MB first.

choices.text: The content of the files sent
choices.why: Intelligence about an address says nothing about what was sent.

choices.text: Proof of who the attacker is
choices.why: An address is not an identity.

prompt: 203.0.113.174 matched an expired indicator with confidence 30. What should the analyst do with that?

choices.text: Block it at once, since it appears in a report
choices.why: Appearing in an expired, low-confidence entry is not a reason.

choices.text: Note it as background noise and act on nothing
choices.why: Right. It explains noise and justifies no action.

choices.text: Ask the sharing group to extend its validity so that the entry is usable again
choices.why: Validity is the author's judgement about their own data.

choices.text: Open an incident for its twelve events
choices.why: Twelve scanning attempts are the internet's ordinary noise.

prompt: In STIX, an indicator for one IPv4 address carries the pattern [___:value = '203.0.113.66'].
hint: The object type for an IPv4 address.

prompt: According to the lesson, what is a SOC's most useful OSINT target?

choices.text: Its own company
choices.why: Right. That is the view an attacker starts from.

choices.text: Staff's private social media in depth
choices.why: Personal data, collected beyond need.

choices.text: Competitors' websites
choices.why: They are not the company's attack surface.

choices.text: The adversary's home network, to learn what tools it runs
choices.why: That is not passive, nor yours; the lesson's limits rule it out.

prompt: The website lists the team, which gave Thursday's visitor real account names. What fix does the lesson favour?

choices.text: Ask the sharing group to remove the names
choices.why: The group did not publish them.

choices.text: Rename every account to a random string
choices.why: That costs daily usability and the names leak anyway.

choices.text: Making names useless on their own: no password-only SSH from the internet
choices.why: Right. Names are not secrets; logins should not depend on them being unknown.

choices.text: Remove the team page from the website
choices.why: The names are also in email and professional networks.

prompt: Which of these stays within the lesson's limits for OSINT?

choices.text: Probing another firm's servers to see what they expose
choices.why: Active, and not yours.

choices.text: Reading certificate transparency logs for the company's own domains
choices.why: Right. Public, passive, and about your own organisation.

choices.text: Building a file on each employee's private life
choices.why: Personal data beyond any defensive need.

choices.text: Logging in to a leaked account of the company's own staff to check whether it still works
choices.why: Using somebody's credentials is not reading public sources.

prompt: What is the usual value of an indicator match, according to the lesson?

choices.text: It tells you what the first clue was
choices.why: Right. It raises confidence and adds context.

choices.text: It proves no other address was involved
choices.why: Absence from a report proves nothing.

choices.text: It identifies the attacker
choices.why: Addresses are not identities.

choices.text: It replaces the need for triage on alerts that involve the matching address
choices.why: Triage still decides; the match is one more piece of context.
